summary:
Chechnya is a republic of Russia and stands under the Russian national framework; the national assessment applies here, but the practical exposure a visitor faces is materially harsher than the national baseline.

Human Rights Watch documented a February 2017 police purge in which men believed to be gay were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. Some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families barely alive from beatings, with captors outing them and urging honour killings. The same reporting establishes that top regional officials knew of the operation despite Ramzan Kadyrov's denial. In late March and early April 2017, Human Rights Watch recorded security forces under Kadyrov rounding up dozens of men suspected of being gay and subjecting them to detention, torture, humiliation, enforced disappearance and severe beatings, with at least three deaths.

Novaya Gazeta reported that more than 100 men were detained across Grozny and other settlements in late March 2017, among them muftiate religious figures and television presenters who had concealed their orientation; at least three detainees were killed and further killings were alleged. Detainees were held in a secret prison in Argun and in multiple detention centres, where they were beaten and tortured with electric shocks; at least three and reportedly up to 20 were beaten to death. Men who were released fled the republic, and users abandoned LGBT messenger groups and closed social-media accounts.

The purge reactivated within two years. A renewed campaign beginning in December 2018 detained around 40 people, including gay men and women, with two killed; by May 2019 police had resumed unlawful detentions, beatings and humiliation of men presumed to be gay or bisexual. In January 2019 Novaya Gazeta learned that warnings were circulating through VKontakte LGBT-group administrators telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov's press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. The paper's April 2017 investigation into the torture and killings produced no criminal case.

Detention has been converted into a conscription channel. The Insider reported in September 2024, citing the monitoring project SK SOS, that Chechen security forces were coercing detained gay men into military service, with at least seven sent to the frontlines in Ukraine and one already killed; the practice began before the 21 September 2022 mobilisation order. In early September 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they would be sent to the front. A Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation recorded a mass wave of unlawful detentions in which people were seized over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse and forced to sign contracts; families sometimes had to recruit two "volunteers" to secure a detained relative's release.

A UK Home Office country policy note of June 2025 records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across Chechnya and the wider North Caucasus between 2017 and 2024, including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

Russian law formally applies in Chechnya, but in practice there are no protections for LGBT residents and visitors, and authorities are alleged to encourage families to kill those suspected of homosexuality. Human Rights Watch found no safe route of complaint or judicial recourse, because retaliation against a complainant was practically inevitable.
tangentialFactors:
Chechnya's own legal order diverges from the framework it sits under. In 1999 the then president Aslan Maskhadov introduced sharia law, under which sharia courts imposed the death penalty for homosexuality and adultery. The current application of Islamic law in the republic contradicts Russian federal law and the Chechen constitution's own provision that Chechnya is secular and that no religion may be made official or mandatory.

External responses have been limited to sanctions. In March 2021 the European Union imposed sanctions on two Chechen government officials over government-sponsored violence against LGBTQIA+ individuals. The UK Home Office note records that the violence associated with the region has spread beyond it.
localsOnly:
For residents, the exposure is continuous rather than episodic. Family and community retaliation is a standing risk: captors have outed detainees to their relatives and urged honour killings, and close social monitoring means that a person suspected of homosexuality can be identified through their own social networks. Those released in 2017 fled the republic, and users abandoned LGBT messenger groups and closed their accounts.

The republic's coercive machinery reaches residents who have no connection to political activity. Memorial's investigation found detentions over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, with detainees taken to police departments, abused and forced to sign military contracts; families were sometimes required to produce two "volunteers" to free a detained relative. Gay men detained on suspicion of homosexuality were sent to the frontlines in Ukraine, with at least seven dispatched and one killed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Death tolls from the 2017 purge are not settled: sources give at least three killed and allege up to 20, and no official accounting exists. The republic has no independent monitoring body or functioning complaint mechanism, so conditions after 2024 are documented only through testimony from people who left and through third-party assessments.

The conflict between the Chechen constitution's secular clause and the application of sharia law has not been resolved by any court, and no Russian or Chechen authority has prosecuted the officials implicated in the 2017 operation.
